newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's most wanted drug baron caught in Quito.
newsitem.headline: Peru's most wanted drug baron caught in Quito.

text.p: The Peruvian government said on Monday police had captured the country's most wanted drug baron in neighbouring Ecuador and had broken up his trafficking ring, which was supplying Colombia's Cali cartel.
"This has been one of the biggest blows against drug- trafficking in recent times," said a triumphant President Alberto Fujimori.

In a joint sting by Peru's intelligence service and Ecuadorean police, Willer Alvarado Linares was arrested in a hotel in Quito during the early hours of Sunday morning after being tracked from the Colombian capital Bogota.
Four other alleged traffickers were arrested with him, and another 41 members of his band were simultaneously arrested in different parts of Peru and Ecuador.
Alvarado was the most powerful Peruvian drug lord at large, controlling the traffic of coca leaf, the raw product for cocaine, in the Amazonian regions around the Colombian border.

Fujimori praised the five-month cross-border operation that led to the arrest. It was codenamed "Eagle" and involved Interpol as well as police and intelligence services in Peru, Colombia and Ecuador.
"I hope that a leader of the calibre of 'Champa' (Alvarado's nickname) receives the tough sentence he deserves," said Fujimori.
He added that the drug lord would be brought back to Peru "between today and tomorrow" where he would be charged and probably receive a sentence "of no less than 25 years."
It was not clear if Alvarado would be charged by a civil court for trafficking or by Peru's secret military court system for alleged collaboration with guerrillas operating in drug-growing areas.

"Champa was also sought by the anti-terrorism police due to proof of his links with the terrorist organisation Shining Path, whom he gave weapons and money in exchange for protection of his illicit activity," said a statement from Government Palace.
Peru, whose economy receives at least $600 million each year from the illegal drugs trade, is the world's largest grower of coca leaf, accounting for at least 50 percent of total production.
